inputs.original_text: They’re pushing changes to Cyprus’ surveillance laws that would strip away judicial oversight—the safeguard that might constrain whoever wants to monitor people. Lawyers are raising concerns, and the amended bill is expected to go to a House vote on Thursday. Akel MP Andreas Pasiourtides mentioned a recent closed session, which only adds to the sense that decisions about surveillance are being handled out of public view. This looks less like routine reform and more like an effort to make scrutiny easier to bypass.
inputs.modified_text: This isn’t just a technical rewrite of Cyprus’ surveillance laws. They’re trying to remove the judicial safeguard that could stop people from being monitored, while lawyers are warning about the changes and the amended bill is expected to go to a House vote on Thursday. Akel MP Andreas Pasiourtides’ mention of a recent closed session makes the pattern harder to ignore: decisions with serious consequences are being kept out of public view, then pushed through as routine reform. The secrecy is part of the point—it makes surveillance easier to expand and scrutiny easier to bypass.
